q1: Distillation helps every student. With the same architecture, the same 5-epoch schedule and the same sequence of mini-batches, the distilled students beat their baselines in top-1 accuracy: MobileNetV2 41.95% → 44.88% (+2.93), EfficientNet-Lite0 43.99% → 47.68% (+3.69), SqueezeNet 42.51% → 42.71% (+0.20). The gain is larger in top-5 accuracy (+3.96, +4.40 and +1.99 points). This is consistent with soft targets passing on the teacher's similarity structure between classes (dark knowledge), and not only its top-1 decision.

Why the gain differs between students. MobileNetV2 and EfficientNet-Lite0 end in 1280-channel feature maps of 2x2. These are close in shape to the teacher's 2048x2x2 layer-4 map, so the 1x1 hint regressor can match them easily and the feature loss gives a useful extra training signal. SqueezeNet has the least capacity (0.78M parameters) and ends in a 512-channel 4x4 map that must be pooled to fit, so it benefits least. This is the familiar capacity gap: a small student cannot copy a much larger teacher closely.

Temperature and the hard/soft balance. With T = 4 the teacher's distribution keeps visible probability on related classes (e.g. the vehicle super-classes of CIFAR-100). The T² factor keeps the gradient of the soft term on the same scale as the CE term. With α = 0.9 most of the signal comes from the teacher, while the 10% hard-label term corrects the teacher's own mistakes (the teacher is 78.5% top-1, not perfect).

Limitations. The teacher was fine-tuned for only 2 epochs and the students were trained for 5 epochs on a CPU, so all absolute accuracies are far below published CIFAR-100 numbers (about 70-75% for these students with 200 epochs). The relative comparison is still controlled: KD and the baseline differ only in the loss. A longer schedule and an ablation of logit-only vs feature-only KD (both supported with --kd-mode) are the obvious next steps.
q2: The constraints shape the search. 69 architectures were generated in 50 minutes. 49 were rejected before any training: 48 for latency above 4 ms and 1 for size above 1 MB. Only 20 were trained. Measuring hardware cost first and rejecting early means no compute was spent on architectures that could not be deployed. For edge NAS this is the main benefit over accuracy-only NAS.

The best architecture. The winner (r24 s32 | 2x16 k3 dsconv SiLU | 2x48 k7 conv LeakyReLU | head 256) uses the smallest input resolution (24x24) and only two stages, which keeps the activation maps small. It combines a cheap depthwise-separable first stage with a dense 7x7 second stage that gives a large receptive field. It reached 53.6% proxy validation accuracy at 1.49 ms latency and 0.66 MB, well inside every constraint. Retrained from scratch on the full 45k training images for 15 epochs, it reaches the test accuracy reported in Section 3.

An honest note on the search dynamics. The best candidate came from the random initial population (#1), and the three fittest architectures were all random. The fittest mutated child reached 49.2% proxy accuracy. With a budget of only 20 trained candidates and 3 proxy epochs on 10k images, the proxy accuracy is noisy (roughly ±2 points). Aging evolution therefore had only 12 mutation steps, too few to improve reliably on a strong random start. With a larger budget (the code supports --budget 100 --epochs 10) the evolutionary phase would have more room to work.

Measurement caveat. For 4 of the 20 trained candidates the fresh-process peak-memory probe failed while the laptop was short on RAM, and their memory was recorded as unknown, not as a violation. Every successfully measured candidate used 4-5 MB, about a third of the 16 MB limit, so this did not affect which candidates were kept. The selected architecture was measured successfully (4.9 MB), and the final benchmark measures it again.
bench: Accuracy versus cost. EfficientNet-Lite0-KD is the most accurate student (47.68% top-1, 80.12% top-5). SqueezeNet is the cheapest to deploy: 2.97 MB as ONNX, 0.74 ms single-thread ORT latency and about 3,000 images/s at batch 64. It is about 5 points less accurate. MobileNetV2-KD sits between the two. All three students are 7-30x smaller than the ResNet-50 teacher (90 MB) and 8-17x faster (12.7 ms), while giving up 31-36 points of accuracy at this short training budget.

Distillation is free at inference time. A KD student has the same parameters, FLOPs, file size and latency as its baseline. The latency differences in the table (<0.1 ms) are measurement noise. The feature-hint regressor is used only during training and is not exported. The +2.9 to +3.7 point accuracy gains therefore cost nothing in deployment.

The NAS model is the most edge-friendly model in the study. At 0.168M parameters and 0.65 MB it is 14x smaller than MobileNetV2. Its single-thread ORT latency is 0.69 ms, and its throughput of 3,277 images/s is the highest measured. After retraining from scratch for 15 epochs it reaches 82.07% top-1 / 99.17% top-5 on the CIFAR-10 test set. It meets every deployment constraint with a wide margin.

PyTorch vs ONNX Runtime. Exported ONNX graphs (opset 17) match PyTorch to within 8e-6 in maximum absolute logit difference, and the top-1 predictions agree 100% for every model. ORT accuracy is therefore identical. At batch 1 on a single thread ORT is 1.9-7.2x faster than PyTorch eager mode (e.g. SqueezeNet 4.62 → 0.74 ms, NAS model 2.33 → 0.69 ms), because ORT fuses Conv+BN+activation and has much lower per-operator overhead. For on-device inference this overhead dominates for small models. Peak memory during inference, measured after the model is loaded, stays below 1.4 MB with ORT and below 6 MB with PyTorch for every model. The teacher's 78.50% (vs 78.52% at training time) comes from storing its checkpoint in fp16.
conclusion: Both frameworks work end to end, from training to ONNX Runtime CPU deployment. Q1 showed that combined logit and feature distillation improves all three lightweight students at zero inference cost, with the largest gains for the higher-capacity students (+3.7 EfficientNet-Lite0, +2.9 MobileNetV2) and only a marginal gain for SqueezeNet. Q2 showed that hardware-in-the-loop NAS with early constraint-based rejection finds a 0.65 MB, sub-millisecond CIFAR-10 model with 82% accuracy, while never training the 71% of candidates that could not be deployed.

The main limitation is compute: all models were trained on a laptop CPU with small epoch budgets. Absolute accuracies are therefore below literature values, and the 20-candidate evolutionary search could not improve on its best random start. All scripts accept larger budgets (README, Section 4). Running them on a GPU, together with a T/α sweep and a logit-only vs feature-only KD ablation, is the natural continuation. Quantising the ONNX models to INT8 would reduce size and latency further for real edge hardware.
